opening.headline: The reason why more cases are blocked when retrying immediately on error 429 is explained using rate limits, error codes, and retry strategies.
body: Let's say some responses came back as 429 during a busy time, and the code sent the same request again as soon as the error occurred. With retry requests added, the number of requests per minute increases, and 429 becomes even more. This is a situation where retrying increases the problem rather than solving it.

In this lesson, we will look at what rate limits are measured by and what error codes mean. We then divide errors that can be retried from those that must be fixed first, and establish standards for judging whether a retry strategy using exponential backoff and retry-after header is safe.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the meaning of rate limits and error codes
Distinguish between retriable and non-retriable errors.
You can determine if your retry strategy is safe

screens.title: I got 429, but I tried again immediately and it blocked even more.
screens.lead: Read the scenes below in chronological order. If we follow how retries affect the number of requests, we can see the structure of the problem.

visual.alt: As time goes by, retry requests are added, increasing the bar for the number of requests per minute.

paragraphs: At 2 PM, due to the influx of requests, some responses returned HTTP 429. 429 means the limit has been exceeded. The app's code was designed to immediately resend the same request if an error occurred.

As a result, retry requests are added to the original request, resulting in higher requests per minute. As the number of requests exceeding the limit increases, the number of 429s increases, and the 429 calls for a retry. This is a structure where retries beget retries.

The Claude document explains that in this case, if there is a `retry-after` header in the response, it will instruct you to wait for that amount of time, and any retry before that time will fail. If so, for some errors you can just wait and retry, and for others it will be useless to resend. The question in this class is how to make that distinction.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Can I retry all errors the same way? At the end of the lesson, you will have a criterion to divide errors into retry possibilities.

screens.outro: First, let's think about my app's retry habits.

screens.title: How do I set the retry interval when an error occurs?
screens.lead: As you select each habit, the instructor's thoughts unfold. First think about which side your app is closer to, then click it. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.answer: This is the simplest method, but also the most dangerous in terms of limit errors. This is because if you send the same amount again right after you have just exceeded the limit, you will immediately exceed the limit again. This method causes the retry congestion seen in the previous screen.

items.prompt: Habit B: Wait for 1 second at a time
items.answer: This is better than an immediate retry, but requests that receive an error at the same time are all regrouped together exactly one second later. In services where there are multiple requests at the same time, the crowding does not disappear but repeats periodically.

items.prompt: Habit C: Waiting longer and longer
items.answer: Increasing the waiting time will spread the crowd over time and give the server time to recover. This is the basic idea of ​​exponential backoff. However, if you apply it to all errors, you will have to wait for errors that are useless even if you retry, so dividing the errors first should be the priority.

screens.outro: Before deciding on a retry, let's check what the limit is measured by.

screens.title: Rate Limits: RPM, TPM and other limits
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the limit metrics and units used by the three providers. The common point is that if any one of the indicators is exceeded, an error occurs.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: Gemini's rate limits are typically measured along three dimensions: requests per minute (RPM), input tokens per minute (TPM), and requests per day (RPD). If any one is exceeded, an error occurs. For example, if the RPM limit is 20 and you send 21 in one minute, an error will occur even if the other limit is not exceeded. Limits apply per project, not per API key.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: OpenAI uses metrics such as RPM, RPD, TPM, TPD (tokens per day), and IPM (images per minute), whichever one reaches first becomes the limit. If the RPM limit is 20, as in the example in the documentation, then sending just 20 requests with only 100 tokens will hit the limit. Response header values ​​such as `x-ratelimit-remaining-requests` and `x-ratelimit-reset-tokens` let you know the remaining amount and time until initialization.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: Claude sets RPM, input token per minute limits (ITPM), and output token per minute limits (OTPM) for each model class. In most models, input tokens read from the cache are not counted in ITPM. The limit is a token bucket type, so the capacity is continuously replenished rather than being reset for each fixed section. So, even if the average usage is below the limit, it can exceed the limit if there is a surge in a short period of time.

tabs.label: common perspective
tabs.body: All three providers fail if just one of several indicators is exceeded, with limits varying depending on the model and tier. Therefore, you should not only count the number of requests, but also manage the number of tokens. This is why you need a retry strategy to break up the crowd.

screens.outro: Let's continue to see what error code occurs when the limit is exceeded.

screens.title: 429 and 5xx: What the error codes mean
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to find the cause and appropriate response for each error code. The last column tells you whether you can retry.

data.caption: Causes for each error code and whether retry is possible
rows: Claude is expressed as `rate_limit_error` and Gemini is expressed as `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`. This is when the per minute limit is exceeded.
You can wait and retry. The only exception is if you have a monthly spending cap.
This is a temporary issue on the server side.
Target for retries with exponential backoff.
Request format, authentication, permissions, and destination issues.
Even if I send it again, the same error occurs. Fix the request or authentication first.
Reduce the request size before sending it.
Payment, input, and authentication limit issues
This is the case when the OpenAI document distinguishes between input, authentication, and payment limit issues.
Resolve the problem first and then try again.
data.notes: All error responses include the request identifier `request_id`, so the Claude documentation tells you to leave this in your error log in case you need to contact us. Whether or not to retry is determined by reading the error type rather than just the first digit of the status code. Even with the same 429, the response to exceeding the per-minute limit and exceeding the monthly spending limit is exactly the opposite.

screens.outro: Now let's see how to read the 429 response line by line and determine the wait time.

screens.title: Read 429 response line by line
screens.lead: 429 Read the response. In the explanation on the right, you can see what each line says and how to set the retry wait time.

notes.note: Status line 429 is limit exceeded. The request itself is correct, so you can just wait and resend.
`retry-after: 12` means that any retry before 12 seconds will fail. If this header is present, this value will take precedence over any manually set latency.
`error.type` in the body indicates the limit type as `rate_limit_error`. `request_id` is the value you leave when making an inquiry.

Even if it is the same `rate_limit_error`, if there is no `retry-after` and there is `enforced_spend_limit_reached`, this is the monthly spending limit. Access will continue to fail until it is freed, including the SDK's automatic retries. In this case, you should stop retrying and check the limit.

screens.outro: The waiting method when there is no header will be summarized as exponential backoff later.

screens.title: Analysis: Retryable and non-retryable errors
screens.lead: As each card is selected, it flips over to reveal a decision and reason. Look at the error on the front of the card, think about whether you can try again, and then flip it over. Move to the next card with the right arrow.

cards.back: Retry is possible. Wait the amount of time given by Heather and send it again. The request itself is correct, and the limit will be restored soon.
Retry is possible. Since it is a temporary overload on the server side, it is re-sent with exponential backoff, increasing the waiting time to 1 second, 2 seconds, 4 seconds, and 8 seconds.
Retrying will not solve the problem. If I send it again with the same key, I get the same error. You must first fix the key and then send it in.
Retrying will not solve the problem. It will continue to fail until access is reopened. You will have to raise the limit or wait until the next cycle and retries will stop.

cards.front: Requests that had side effects during 500 errors
cards.back: Requests that have side effects, such as payments or file changes, are retried after checking the results first. This is because even if an error occurs, the previous part may have already been executed. Retrying without confirmation may cause problems such as the same payment being made twice.
Retrying as is will not solve the problem. This error occurred because the request was larger than the limit, so you should reduce or split the content you are sending.

screens.outro: Now that we have established the classification criteria, let's read and fix the poor retry code ourselves.

screens.title: Commentary: Reading and fixing poor retry code
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow the instructor as he finds and fixes problem lines in the retry loop, one by one. The symptom is that after 100 simultaneous requests, 429 is received and then 429 is continuously received.

steps.title: Step 1: Read the code
steps.body:
The code in question looks like this:

```python
while True:
    res = send(request)
    if res.status == 200:
        break
    sleep(1)
```

If the response is not 200, rest for 1 second and repeat infinitely. If 100 simultaneous requests receive 429, the same amount will be received at once every second, and 429 will continue to appear.

steps.title: Step 2 Line-by-Line Cause 1: Retry all errors
steps.body: The condition `other than 200` will also retry errors such as 401 or 400. This error occurs even if the same request is sent again. Narrow the retry targets to 429, 500, and 529.

steps.title: Step 3 Line-by-Line Cause 2: Static Wait
steps.body: Pinning `sleep(1)` causes all requests that received an error to be redirected at the same time. Increase the wait time to something like 1 second, 2 seconds, 4 seconds, and add random variation to each request to break up the crowd.

steps.title: Step 4 Line-by-Line Cause 3: Header and Count
steps.body: No reading of `retry-after` and no limit on number of attempts. If there is a header, that value takes precedence, and backoff is used only if there is no header. Prevent infinite repetition by setting a maximum number of attempts and an overall deadline. The Claude SDK backoff retries twice by default and follows `retry-after`.

steps.title: Results of 5 steps of correction
steps.body: The fixed loop picks only retryable errors and waits with `retry-after` or exponential backoff, placing an upper limit on the number of attempts. In addition, the number of concurrent executions is limited to reduce the number of requests that are rushed at once. If you don't have `retry-after` and it keeps failing, like the monthly spending cap of 429, stop retrying and check the limit.

screens.outro: Now that I've finished editing, I'll close by summarizing the main points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Errors are divided by retryability
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. Find out the answer to the original question: which errors should be retried and which should not be retried.

paragraphs: To answer your initial question, the error is divided by the retry probability. Errors that can be resolved by waiting, such as 429, 500, and 529, are retried, and errors in which the request or authentication is incorrect, such as 400, 401, 403, and 404, are corrected first. 413 requires reducing the request size, and requests that had side effects should be retried after checking the results.

Three retry strategies are used together. If the response contains `retry-after`, that time takes precedence. If not, exponential backoff increases latency and adds random deviation to break up the herd. And set the maximum number of attempts to prevent infinite repetition.

To prevent a flood of retries, limit the number of concurrent requests. Even if it is the same `rate_limit_error`, there is no monthly spending limit `retry-after` and it keeps failing, so stop retrying and check the limit. Leave `request_id` in all error responses in the log.

callout.label: distinction to remember
callout.text: Retry for errors that can be resolved by waiting, and fix errors that require fixing. Retries come with headers, backoffs, count limits, and concurrency limits.

glossary.def: Usage limits set by requests per minute (RPM), tokens per minute (TPM), etc. If any one of the indicators is exceeded, an error occurs.
429 is a limit exceeded, 5xx (500, 529, etc.) is a temporary issue on the server side. This is something to wait for and then retry.
Each retry doubles the waiting time and sets a maximum number of attempts.
Header like retry-after. It tells you the minimum waiting time before you can try again.

misconceptions.myth: If an error occurs, the fastest way is to retry immediately.
misconceptions.fact: Immediate retries further exhaust the limit, increasing blocking. You must wait and retry.

misconceptions.myth: All errors are resolved by retrying.
misconceptions.fact: Requests such as 400 or 401 or authentication issues will result in the same error even if you resend the same request. You have to fix it first.

misconceptions.myth: All 429s will be solved if you wait a moment.
misconceptions.fact: 429s that have reached their monthly spending cap have no retry-after and will continue to fail until access is released. In this case, you should check the limit.

misconceptions.myth: When 429 comes, you can always wait with retry-after.
misconceptions.fact: You need to read the error_code of the response and the presence or absence of retry-after to determine whether the monthly spending is capped.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The error is divided by the retry probability.
429 and 5xx wait and retry, while 400 series fix the request first.
We use retry-after, exponential backoff, and maximum number of attempts together.
Prevents retry flooding by limiting the number of concurrent requests.
